caption:
Synthetic-aperture radar can see through cloud cover and darkness, which is why it works for flood-prone river reaches during rainy season when optical imagery is useless. It measures changes in water extent and surface roughness along a monitored reach and flags deviations from the historical pattern.

The honest limit: this is a periodic sample, not continuous surveillance. Each pass gives a snapshot at a fixed revisit interval. Between passes, the reach can change and we will not see it until the next acquisition. This is not a live camera feed. It is a repeated measurement, useful because the intervals are short enough to catch a rising signature before it becomes a headline.

When we ran the array back against the September 2022 Numan flood, it flagged the signature four days before the official warning went out. The 2021 control year, with no flood, correctly stayed quiet. That is the proof point we have. We are not claiming more than that.
thread: Synthetic-aperture radar sees through cloud and dark, which matters for flood monitoring during rainy season when optical imagery goes blind.
But it's a periodic sample, not continuous surveillance. Each pass is a snapshot at a fixed revisit interval. Between passes, conditions on a reach can shift before we see it again.
Run back against the real September 2022 Numan flood, the reach-monitoring array flagged the signature four days before the official warning. The 2021 control year stayed quiet, correctly.
That's the one hindcast we point to. We don't claim a second one, and we don't claim to watch every reach at every hour.

card.headline: A periodic sample, not a live feed
card.sub: Radar sees through cloud and dark on a fixed revisit interval. It caught the Numan flood signature four days early. It cannot see between passes.

rationale: Leads with a real, differentiated capability (radar's all-weather advantage) and immediately caps it with the periodic-sampling limit, then earns trust with the single approved proof point instead of overclaiming.
